controls.name: Symmetric Encryption
controls.description: General implementation of symmetric encryption using a shared secret key for confidentiality. Applicable to in-vehicle communication channels and data-at-rest protection. This is a high-level control that should be refined by specific algorithm implementations.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forces the attacker to perform cryptanalysis or side-channel key extraction against the underlying cipher, a sustained effort typically measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Practical cryptanalysis or side-channel key recovery against a modern symmetric cipher requires genuine applied-cryptography expertise, not casual scripting.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The specific cipher mode and key-management scheme used by a given implementation are not published, but are discoverable through reverse engineering rather than deeply proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once a ciphertext sample is captured, cryptanalysis or brute-force key search proceeds entirely offline with no further access-window constraint.

equipment.rationale: Side-channel extraction typically requires bespoke physical equipment (oscilloscopes, probes).

controls.name: AES (Advanced Encryption Standard)
controls.description: AES block cipher implementation. Provides high-security confidentiality for automotive data-at-rest and in-transit. Often hardware-accelerated to maintain real-time performance on ECUs.

elapsedTime.rationale: AES is computationally infeasible to brute force within reasonable timeframes.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires deep knowledge of block cipher implementation and side-channel analysis.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: AES itself is a fully public FIPS-197 standard; defeating a specific deployment requires only implementation-level details (key size, mode, hardware-acceleration leakage) rather than confidential algorithm knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Captured ciphertext can be attacked offline at any time; the algorithm's strength does not depend on catching a live window.

equipment.rationale: Logical brute force is computationally infeasible; recovering the key in practice requires bespoke side-channel equipment (EM probes, oscilloscopes) against the hardware accelerator.

controls.name: ChaCha20
controls.description: ChaCha20 stream cipher. Offers high performance in software-only environments (no hardware acceleration needed) while maintaining robust resistance against timing attacks.

elapsedTime.rationale: High computational complexity for state recovery.

specialistExpertise.rationale: State recovery or differential attacks against a modern stream cipher require deep applied-cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The algorithm is a public IETF standard (RFC 8439); a practical attack requires only knowledge of the implementation's nonce/counter management, not secret algorithm internals.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: As a pure software cipher, captured ciphertext can be analyzed offline at leisure with no access-window constraint.

equipment.rationale: Less susceptible to hardware-based EM/Power side channels if purely software-based, standard IT tools apply.

controls.name: Asymmetric Encryption
controls.description: Asymmetric encryption uses public/private key pairs for secure key exchange, authentication, and digital signatures in automotive systems. It is essential for secure OTA updates, V2X communications, and establishing trust between ECUs and backend servers.

elapsedTime.rationale: Recovering a private key or forging a valid handshake against modern asymmetric primitives requires sustained cryptanalytic or implementation-flaw research, typically months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting padding, parameter, or protocol weaknesses in asymmetric key exchange/signing requires genuine public-key cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Defeating a specific deployment requires knowledge of the OEM's chosen key sizes, padding scheme, and PKI trust-chain configuration, which is not publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Private-key extraction or mathematical cryptanalysis can largely be pursued offline once public key material is obtained; only implementation-flaw exploitation requires timing against a live exchange.

equipment.rationale: Commodity MITM/proxy tooling and moderate compute suffice once a cryptographic or implementation weakness is identified.

controls.name: RSA (Rivest-Shamir-Adleman)
controls.description: RSA is a foundational asymmetric cryptographic algorithm used for secure data transmission, digital signatures, and secure boot in automotive ECUs.

elapsedTime.rationale: RSA at automotive-grade key sizes is computationally infeasible to factor within reasonable timeframes.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Padding-oracle or implementation attacks (e.g., Bleichenbacher-style) against RSA require applied-cryptography expertise; direct factoring at automotive key sizes is infeasible.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: RSA is a fully public algorithm; the only implementation-specific knowledge needed is the padding scheme and key size in use, which are moderately restricted rather than confidential.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The public modulus is available for offline factoring/attack attempts at any time; only oracle-style implementation attacks require live query access to the target.

equipment.rationale: Commodity high-performance computing supports implementation-flaw attacks; physical key extraction would additionally require side-channel equipment.

controls.name: ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography)
controls.description: ECC is an efficient asymmetric cryptography method used for secure key exchange and digital signatures in resource-constrained automotive ECUs. ECC provides equivalent security to RSA with smaller key sizes.

elapsedTime.rationale: Solving the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem at automotive-grade curve sizes is computationally infeasible within reasonable timeframes.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting weak curve parameters, invalid-curve attacks, or nonce reuse against ECC requires deep elliptic-curve cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The curve and signature scheme are typically standard/public; only the specific parameter choice and nonce-generation implementation are restricted.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Public key material can be attacked offline; only invalid-curve or fault-based attacks require live interaction with the target device.

equipment.rationale: Standard compute suffices for cryptanalysis; side-channel/fault attacks against embedded ECC implementations require bespoke probing equipment.

controls.name: Network Security
controls.description: Foundational controls designed to protect automotive and cloud-connected systems from network-based threats. Includes measures such as network segmentation, traffic monitoring, and secure communication baselines.

elapsedTime.rationale: Represents baseline hygiene (segmentation, monitoring, secure baselines); a proficient attacker can map and probe a modestly hardened network within weeks.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic network reconnaissance and off-the-shelf scanning/exploitation tools suffice against generic baseline controls.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires only moderately restricted knowledge of the network topology, not deep proprietary design detail.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Baseline controls do not meaningfully restrict access timing; the attacker can probe the network whenever it is reachable.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard IT networking and penetration-testing tools.

controls.name: TLS (Transport Layer Security)
controls.description: TLS is a cryptographic protocol for securing data in transit over automotive networks, including backend communications, OTA updates, and telematics. TLS 1.3 provides forward secrecy by default.

elapsedTime.rationale: Exploiting TLS requires either compromising key material or discovering a genuine protocol/implementation weakness, typically taking months of sustained effort.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting TLS requires either a certificate/key compromise or genuine protocol-level attack expertise (downgrade, implementation CVEs); forward secrecy in TLS 1.3 defeats simple key-obtained-later attacks.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific cipher-suite negotiation, certificate-validation logic, and pinning behavior implemented by the target client/server.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A live on-path position must be held through the handshake before session keys are established; once complete, forward secrecy closes the window.

equipment.rationale: Standard MITM/proxy tooling (mitmproxy, custom relays) is sufficient; no specialized hardware is required for a logical attack.

controls.name: Rate Limiting
controls.description: Rate limiting restricts the number of requests or messages allowed over a network interface. In vehicles, it prevents DoS attacks on the CAN bus or CPU exhaustion on ECUs.

elapsedTime.rationale: Rate limits are commonly bypassed within days by rotating source identifiers or spreading requests across many origins.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Evasion via IP/ID rotation or distributed sourcing is a well-known, low-skill technique.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires only the target's rate threshold, discoverable through observation/probing rather than confidential design knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The rate-limited interface is continuously reachable whenever the system is operating; no special timing is needed to attempt evasion.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard flooding/scripting tools or a small botnet-for-hire.

controls.name: Autoscaling
controls.description: Autoscaling automatically adjusts the number of active resources in cloud environments based on demand, ensuring resilience against traffic spikes and DoS attacks.

elapsedTime.rationale: Outpacing autoscaling requires sustaining a volumetric attack that exceeds the scaling budget/limits, typically requiring weeks of buildup.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Volumetric DDoS techniques are widely available and require limited specialist skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the backend's scaling limits/budget, which is operational information restricted to the operator, not deeply secret.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The backend endpoint is continuously reachable while operating; no narrow access window applies.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with commodity load-generation/botnet tooling.

controls.name: Network Segmentation
controls.description: Divides automotive networks into isolated segments (e.g., VLANs, physically separate buses), limiting the spread of attacks and restricting lateral movement.

elapsedTime.rationale: Discovering and exploiting a segmentation gap or bridging misconfiguration is achievable within weeks by a determined attacker.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine understanding of the specific VLAN/bus topology to identify a viable pivot point between segments.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The OEM's specific segmentation architecture and inter-segment gateway rules are proprietary and not published.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The attacker must first establish a foothold on one segment and pivot before detection, bounding the available window.

equipment.rationale: Lateral movement uses standard network reconnaissance and pivoting tools once a foothold exists.

controls.name: Certificate Management and Revocation
controls.description: Ensures digital certificates used for authentication, encryption, and signing in automotive systems are properly issued, renewed, and revoked (e.g., via CRLs or OCSP). Essential for maintaining trust in V2X and OTA.

elapsedTime.rationale: Exploiting revocation gaps (OCSP soft-fail, CRL propagation lag) to use a compromised credential undetected takes sustained effort to locate and time.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting revocation gaps (OCSP soft-fail, CRL propagation lag) requires genuine PKI operational expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific revocation-checking behavior (soft-fail vs hard-fail, CRL refresh interval) implemented by the target.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The attack is only viable within the propagation delay between key compromise and CRL/OCSP update reaching all relying parties.

equipment.rationale: A purely logical/protocol-level attack; no specialized hardware is required.

controls.name: MACsec (Media Access Control Security)
controls.description: MACsec provides encryption and integrity protection at the data link layer for automotive Ethernet networks, securing high-speed in-vehicle communications (e.g., Zonal controllers to Central Compute).

elapsedTime.rationale: Compromising MACsec-protected links requires months of sustained effort against either the MKA key-agreement protocol or physical tap-and-extract of the key.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Compromising MACsec requires expertise in the MKA key-agreement protocol or Ethernet frame-level cryptography.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The specific cipher suite and key-rotation cadence used on the vehicle's Ethernet backbone are proprietary to the OEM's zonal architecture.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access to the high-speed Ethernet backbone (often behind zonal controllers) is only available during specific service/maintenance windows.

equipment.rationale: Intercepting MACsec requires physical access to the high-speed Ethernet lines and specialized network tapping gear.

controls.name: Secure Key Encapsulation / Exchange
controls.description: Secure key encapsulation and exchange mechanisms provide the foundation for establishing cryptographic session keys over insecure automotive networks, reinforcing network security by protecting key material during transport and session setup.

elapsedTime.rationale: Breaking the underlying hard math problem for classical key exchange takes sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exchange-substitution or small-subgroup attacks require applied-cryptography protocol expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific exchange parameters and session-establishment flow used by the target implementation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The attacker must be positioned to intercept or tamper with the live exchange before session keys are finalized.

equipment.rationale: Requires network-tap/relay hardware to intercept and manipulate the exchange in real time.

controls.name: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
controls.description: Diffie-Hellman is a protocol for securely exchanging cryptographic keys over insecure automotive networks, enabling secure session establishment. Often used as part of TLS handshakes or V2X.

elapsedTime.rationale: Breaking the discrete-logarithm problem for classical Diffie-Hellman groups at automotive-appropriate sizes takes sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: MITM substitution or small-subgroup confinement attacks against unauthenticated DH require protocol-level cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: DH group parameters are typically drawn from public standards (e.g., RFC 3526); no confidential algorithm knowledge is needed beyond the public transcript.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A live on-path position is required during the handshake to substitute key material before both sides derive the shared secret.

equipment.rationale: Standard network MITM tooling is sufficient for classic key-substitution attacks.

controls.name: ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism)
controls.description: ML-KEM (formerly Kyber) is a post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism based on the module learning-with-errors problem. It provides a quantum-resistant method for secure key establishment, protecting automotive communication channels against 'harvest now, decrypt later' quantum attacks.

elapsedTime.rationale: High resistance to cryptanalytic efforts even with quantum acceleration.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Implementation and analysis of lattice-based KEMs require specialized cryptographic expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: ML-KEM's algorithm and parameter sets are fully public NIST FIPS 203 specifications; no confidential knowledge of a specific implementation is required to mount a cryptanalytic attack, only advanced lattice-cryptography expertise (captured separately).

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once the encapsulation ciphertext is captured, lattice-based cryptanalysis proceeds entirely offline with no further access-window constraint.

equipment.rationale: Standard high-end compute capability; no specialized quantum hardware required for defensive implementation.

controls.name: Firewall
controls.description: A firewall monitors and controls incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predetermined rules. In automotive systems, firewalls (often running on the central gateway) segment networks and block unauthorized access.

elapsedTime.rationale: Identifying gaps in filter rules or viable protocol-tunneling paths through a gateway firewall typically takes a few weeks of probing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: As the central automotive gateway (not a generic perimeter box), bypassing its stateful inspection typically requires genuine protocol-tunneling or fragmentation expertise rather than simple rule gaps.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific rule set deployed on the gateway, which is operational configuration rather than deep proprietary design.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The firewall is continuously active whenever the network is powered, so probing can occur at any time the vehicle/backend is reachable.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard network scanning and tunneling tools.

controls.name: Load Balancer
controls.description: A load balancer distributes incoming network traffic across multiple servers. In connected vehicle ecosystems, load balancers help mitigate denial-of-service attacks on backend infrastructure.

elapsedTime.rationale: A sufficiently large volumetric or slow application-layer attack can exhaust load-balancer capacity within weeks of buildup.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic DDoS/slow-loris techniques are widely documented and require limited specialist skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the backend's capacity/health-check thresholds, which is operational rather than confidential.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The load-balanced endpoint is continuously reachable while the backend is operating.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with commodity load-generation tooling.

controls.name: Intrusion Detection System (IDS)
controls.description: An IDS monitors network or system activities for malicious actions or policy violations. It does not actively block traffic, but alerts the SOC. Forces an attacker to use slow, evasive techniques to avoid detection.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forces the attacker to use 'low and slow' evasion techniques.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires advanced knowledge of IDS evasion (fragmentation, timing).

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific detection signatures/thresholds tuned by the SOC, which is restricted operational configuration, not published.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The network is continuously monitored while operating, so evasion is not tied to a narrow timing window - the technique must work whenever traffic is sent.

equipment.rationale: Evasion is achieved through traffic-shaping/timing techniques using standard software tools, with no special hardware.

controls.name: Intrusion Prevention System (IPS)
controls.description: An IPS actively analyzes and takes automated actions to block or prevent detected threats in network traffic, such as dropping malicious packets or quarantining a compromised node.

elapsedTime.rationale: Evading active blocking (not just detection) requires developing genuinely novel evasion techniques or exploiting a blind spot in the IPS's inline decision logic, taking substantially longer than passive IDS evasion.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires protocol-ambiguity or fragmentation techniques specifically engineered to defeat inline blocking decisions, not just detection signatures.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific IPS's blocking rules and thresholds, which are operationally restricted but not deeply proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The IPS is continuously active whenever the network is powered, so the evasion technique is not tied to a narrow timing window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard traffic-crafting software tools.

controls.name: Automotive IVN Intrusion Detection (CAN / Ethernet IDPS)
controls.description: Bus-level anomaly detection for in-vehicle networks, monitoring CAN message frequency, timing patterns, unexpected transmitter IDs, and Ethernet payload anomalies against the vehicle's expected communication matrix. Distinct from IP-layer IDS (C.03.10) which targets backend connectivity - this control targets automotive-specific protocol anomalies as required by UN R155 mitigation categories M6 and M15.

elapsedTime.rationale: Attacker must craft messages that blend into the normal traffic baseline, requiring deep knowledge of the vehicle's communication matrix (DBC/ARXML).

specialistExpertise.rationale: Blending malicious CAN/Ethernet traffic into the expected communication-matrix baseline requires genuine expertise in automotive bus protocols and the target's specific timing/frequency profile.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires the vehicle's specific DBC/ARXML communication matrix (message IDs, expected frequency, signal ranges), which is proprietary OEM engineering data, not publicly published.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The bus is continuously monitored while the vehicle is operating, but injected messages must match the expected timing window to avoid frequency-anomaly flags.

equipment.rationale: Requires a CAN/Ethernet interface capable of precisely timed frame injection (e.g., programmable CAN transceiver), beyond a basic OBD dongle.

controls.name: TLS/Cipher Downgrade Prevention & Protocol Version Enforcement
controls.description: Enforces a strict minimum negotiable TLS/DTLS protocol version (TLS 1.2 minimum, TLS 1.3 preferred) and an explicit allow-list of strong cipher suites at every backend, OTA, and ISO 15118 V2G/EVSE endpoint, rejecting connection attempts that request deprecated versions (SSLv3, TLS 1.0/1.1) or export-grade/weak ciphers. Implements anti-downgrade signaling - the TLS 1.3 downgrade sentinel value in ServerHello.random and/or RFC 7507's TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV - so an active on-path attacker cannot silently coerce a fallback to a weaker protocol without the fallback being detected and rejected. Combines this with certificate/public-key pinning on high-value channels (OTA distribution, V2G Plug & Charge) so that a downgraded handshake still cannot complete against an attacker-controlled endpoint even if a rogue CA is otherwise trusted.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forces the attacker to find an implementation-level bypass (e.g., a client that silently ignores the downgrade sentinel or a pinning misconfiguration) rather than perform a simple handshake manipulation, substantially lengthening the effort required.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Defeating certificate pinning combined with strict version/cipher enforcement requires either a compromised CA/private key or a genuine implementation flaw, not generic MITM tooling.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires detailed knowledge of the specific TLS stack's version-negotiation and pinning implementation to locate an exploitable inconsistency.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A MITM position alone is no longer sufficient; the position must be held while a separate implementation or trust-chain weakness is located and exploited.

equipment.rationale: Still achievable with commodity MITM/proxy tooling once a bypass vector has been identified, but the tooling alone no longer succeeds against a compliant endpoint.

controls.notes: Directly denies the mechanism modeled by T.01.13 (Cryptographic/Transport Protocol Downgrade Attack).

controls.name: Hashing
controls.description: Hashing transforms data into a fixed-size digest. Used for verifying firmware and diagnostic-message integrity, supporting secure boot verification, and detecting data tampering. As a keyless mechanism, hashing alone establishes integrity, not sender authentication - that requires pairing it with a secret key (MAC, C.06) or a signature (C.05).

elapsedTime.rationale: As a generic parent control, the specific algorithm strength is not committed; assuming at least a modern hash function, finding a practical collision/preimage takes weeks of targeted compute.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Generic hash manipulation (e.g., appending garbage, exploiting a weak/legacy choice) requires only modest technical skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowing which hash function and whether a salt/context value is used, which is restricted implementation detail.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A captured hash value can be attacked offline (collision search, precomputed tables) with no timing constraint.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard computing hardware and public hash-cracking tools.

controls.name: SHA-2 Family
controls.description: The SHA-2 family consists of cryptographic hash functions including SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512, which are based on the Merkle-Damgård construction.

elapsedTime.rationale: No practical collision or preimage attack exists against SHA-256/512 at automotive-relevant scale; any progress requires sustained cryptanalytic research.

specialistExpertise.rationale: No practical collision or preimage attack exists against SHA-256/512; only theoretical cryptanalysis by specialists narrows the security margin.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: SHA-2 is a fully public FIPS 180-4 standard; no confidential knowledge of a specific implementation is needed to attempt cryptanalysis.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A captured hash digest can be attacked offline indefinitely; there is no live-access constraint.

equipment.rationale: Cryptanalytic research against SHA-2 uses standard computing resources; no specialized equipment provides a meaningful advantage.

controls.name: SHA-3 Family
controls.description: SHA-3 is a modern cryptographic hash function based on the Keccak algorithm. Uses a sponge construction, making it resistant to length extension attacks.

elapsedTime.rationale: The sponge construction underlying SHA-3 has an even larger security margin than SHA-2 against known cryptanalytic techniques, including length-extension.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Analyzing the Keccak sponge construction for exploitable weaknesses requires genuine cryptanalytic expertise, though none is currently known to be practical.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: SHA-3 is a fully public FIPS 202 standard; the sponge construction is documented and requires no confidential implementation knowledge to attack.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Digests can be analyzed offline at any time once captured.

equipment.rationale: Standard computing resources suffice for any cryptanalytic attempt.

controls.name: MD5
controls.description: MD5 is a legacy hash function sometimes found in older automotive systems. Due to known vulnerabilities (high collision probability), it should be replaced by stronger algorithms.

elapsedTime.rationale: Collisions can be generated in seconds using standard IT equipment.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Publicly available chosen-prefix collision tools (e.g., HashClash) require only modest scripting skill to run.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: MD5 collision generation is a fully public, well-documented technique requiring no knowledge of the specific target implementation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A collision can be pre-computed entirely offline before ever interacting with the target system.

equipment.rationale: Achievable on a standard laptop; no specialized hardware needed.

controls.notes: DEPRECATED. MD5 is cryptographically broken: practical chosen-prefix collision attacks are achievable in seconds on commodity hardware (~2^18 operations). This entry exists solely to model legacy system residual risk. Any new design using MD5 for integrity protection violates UN R155 security principles. Migrate immediately to SHA-256 or SHA-3.

controls.name: Digital Signature
controls.description: Digital signatures provide a cryptographic means to verify the authenticity and integrity of messages, firmware, or software in automotive systems. Foundational for secure boot, OTA updates, and authenticated diagnostics.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forging a valid signature via cryptanalysis or private-key extraction against a modern signature scheme requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine public-key cryptography expertise to exploit weak randomness, malleability, or implementation flaws in signature verification.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific signature algorithm, key management, and verification-chain configuration used by the OEM, which is not published.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once a signed artifact and its public key are available, cryptanalytic or key-extraction attacks largely proceed offline.

equipment.rationale: Commodity compute supports implementation-flaw exploitation; physical key extraction additionally requires side-channel equipment.

controls.name: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm)
controls.description: DSA is a standard for generating and verifying digital signatures, used to authenticate firmware, software, and messages in automotive ECUs.

elapsedTime.rationale: Exploiting DSA's known sensitivity to nonce reuse or biased randomness to recover the private key takes sustained analysis of collected signatures.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting DSA's well-known sensitivity to nonce reuse or biased randomness requires genuine applied-cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: DSA is a public standard; the main implementation-specific knowledge needed is the RNG/nonce-generation approach, which is restricted but not deeply proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Signed messages and public keys can be collected and analyzed offline for nonce-reuse patterns without needing continuous live access.

equipment.rationale: Standard compute suffices for nonce-bias analysis; physical key extraction would additionally require side-channel equipment.

controls.name: ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm)
controls.description: ECDSA is a digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curve cryptography, providing strong security with smaller key sizes. Widely used in automotive V2X, secure diagnostics, and OTA update authentication.

elapsedTime.rationale: Recovering the ECDSA private key via nonce-bias analysis or fault injection requires sustained effort collecting and analyzing signatures or physical access.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting ECDSA nonce reuse, weak curve parameters, or fault-injection to recover the private key requires deep elliptic-curve cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The curve and hash-to-scalar mapping are typically standardized/public; only the specific RNG implementation is restricted knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Collected signatures can be analyzed offline for nonce bias; only fault-injection attacks require live physical access.

equipment.rationale: Nonce-bias cryptanalysis needs only standard compute; physical fault injection requires bespoke voltage/clock glitching equipment.

controls.name: EdDSA (Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm)
controls.description: EdDSA is a modern digital signature algorithm designed for high performance and security. It offers inherent resistance to side-channel attacks and nonce-reuse vulnerabilities, making it highly recommended for automotive designs.

elapsedTime.rationale: EdDSA's deterministic nonces remove the classic randomness-reuse attack path, requiring the attacker to pursue slower fault-based or cryptanalytic routes.

specialistExpertise.rationale: EdDSA's deterministic nonce generation removes the classic randomness-reuse attack surface, so defeating it requires deeper cryptanalytic or fault-based expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: EdDSA (Ed25519/Ed448) is a fully public standard; only the specific deployment's key management is restricted, non-public information.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: EdDSA's deterministic nonces eliminate the reuse-based attack window; any successful cryptanalysis of collected signatures can proceed entirely offline.

equipment.rationale: Standard compute suffices for cryptanalysis; extracting the key via physical fault injection requires bespoke glitching equipment.

controls.name: ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard)
controls.description: ML-DSA (formerly Dilithium) is a post-quantum digital signature algorithm based on the hardness of module-lattice problems. It provides quantum-resistant authenticity, integrity, and non-repudiation, making it suitable for future-proof automotive applications like V2X and secure OTA.

elapsedTime.rationale: Breaking lattice-based signatures requires significant computational resources, resistant to quantum speedups.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires advanced knowledge of lattice cryptography and quantum-safe protocols.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: ML-DSA's algorithm and parameter sets are fully public NIST FIPS 204 specifications; no confidential implementation knowledge is required to attempt cryptanalysis.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Collected signatures can be analyzed entirely offline using publicly known lattice-cryptanalysis techniques, with no live access-window constraint.

equipment.rationale: Standard high-performance computing is sufficient, but brute force is infeasible.

controls.name: Message Authentication Codes
controls.description: A Message Authentication Code (MAC) is a short piece of information, computed using a shared secret key, that lets the recipient verify both the integrity and authenticity of a message.

elapsedTime.rationale: As a generic parent, assuming at least baseline keyed authentication, forging a valid tag without the key takes at least weeks of targeted effort against a shorter/generic construction.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic MAC forgery attempts (e.g., length-extension against improperly constructed schemes) require only moderate skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific MAC construction and key size used, restricted implementation detail.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Captured message/MAC pairs can be analyzed offline for forgery weaknesses without further access to the live bus.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard computing and CAN-analysis software.

controls.name: HMAC (Hash-Based Message Authentication Code)
controls.description: HMAC verifies the integrity and authenticity of messages exchanged between ECUs using a cryptographic hash function and a secret key.

elapsedTime.rationale: HMAC's construction resists length-extension attacks; forging a valid tag without the key requires breaking the underlying hash function itself, a genuine cryptanalytic undertaking.

specialistExpertise.rationale: HMAC's resistance to length-extension means forging a valid tag requires breaking the underlying hash function, a genuine cryptanalytic undertaking.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: HMAC is a fully public construction (RFC 2104); the only restricted knowledge is the specific hash function and key length chosen.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Captured message/tag pairs can be analyzed offline indefinitely; there is no live timing constraint on the cryptanalysis itself.

equipment.rationale: A purely computational attack; no specialized equipment improves the odds against a well-implemented HMAC.

controls.name: CMAC (Cipher-based Message Authentication Code)
controls.description: CMAC is a symmetric-key algorithm based on block ciphers like AES, used for message authentication and integrity verification in automotive networks. It is susceptible to block-cipher side-channel attacks if implemented purely in generic hardware.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forging a CMAC tag without the key requires either breaking the underlying block cipher or successfully mounting a side-channel key-recovery campaign, both taking sustained effort.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Forging a CMAC tag requires either breaking the underlying block cipher or exploiting block-cipher side-channel leakage, both requiring genuine cryptographic expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: CMAC is a public NIST SP 800-38B construction; only the underlying block cipher and key size are implementation-specific restricted knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Side-channel key extraction requires repeated physical measurements against the live device, imposing a mild but real access constraint beyond pure offline cryptanalysis.

equipment.rationale: As flagged by its susceptibility to block-cipher side channels in generic hardware, practical key recovery requires oscilloscopes/EM probes rather than pure computation.

controls.name: Secure Onboard Communication (SecOC)
controls.description: AUTOSAR SecOC provides MAC-based message authentication for CAN and SOME/IP frames, ensuring every PDU originates from a trusted sender. It is the primary IVN-level control against replay and injection attacks on the CAN bus. This is a foundational refinement of C.06 applied to the automotive network layer.

elapsedTime.rationale: Attacker must first obtain the shared SecOC symmetric key before forging any authenticated frame.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires knowledge of AUTOSAR SecOC PDU layout, counter management, and CAN bus tooling.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific AUTOSAR SecOC configuration (Freshness Value length/management, PDU authenticator length, per-ECU key assignment), which is proprietary OEM engineering data not publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Both the live CAN bus (for injection attempts) and the freshness/counter synchronization window must be caught before a forged frame is rejected as stale, moderately bounding the attack window.

equipment.rationale: CAN interface required for injection attempts; key extraction additionally requires SCA or debug equipment.

controls.name: Trusted Execution Environment
controls.description: A Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) is a secure area of a processor that ensures sensitive code and data are isolated from the main operating system. In automotive systems, TEEs protect cryptographic operations, key storage, and security-critical applications from compromise, even if the main OS is attacked.

elapsedTime.rationale: Breaking TEE isolation, whether via a logical exploit of the secure-monitor interface or basic physical glitching, requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Breaking TEE isolation via a logical exploit (compromised secure monitor call handling) or basic voltage glitching requires genuine embedded-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific TEE OS/secure-monitor implementation (e.g., OP-TEE, proprietary vendor TEE) and its API surface, which is not publicly documented for a given SoC.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Logical attacks against the TEE's API can be attempted whenever the device is powered on; only physical fault injection meaningfully narrows the window to moments of active secure-operation execution.

equipment.rationale: Logical attacks require standard IT equipment; physical glitching requires specialized voltage/clock injection tools.

controls.name: Enclave Runtime Environment
controls.description: The secure software layer or microkernel running within an isolated execution state. It manages secure applications, exposes hardened APIs, and validates boundaries to shield critical logic from the primary OS.

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding and weaponizing a logic flaw in the trusted API's Secure Monitor Call handling takes sustained vulnerability-research effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting the enclave runtime via malformed Secure Monitor Calls or logic flaws in the trusted API requires genuine secure-OS exploitation expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires detailed knowledge of the specific enclave runtime's SMC interface and API validation logic, which is vendor-proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The SMC interface is reachable whenever the rich OS is running, so logical exploitation is not tied to a narrow timing window.

equipment.rationale: Attacking the enclave runtime environment is typically a logical software exploitation exercise via Secure Monitor Calls (SMC).

controls.name: Hardware-Enforced Domain Isolation
controls.description: Silicon-level security mechanisms (such as hardware security extensions, memory encryption, or hardware-based privilege separation) that enforce isolated memory spaces and execution states at the physical layer.

elapsedTime.rationale: Defeating a silicon-level isolation mechanism through fault injection or decapsulation-based analysis takes sustained lab effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Defeating a silicon-level isolation mechanism requires advanced hardware fault-injection or decapsulation expertise, typically beyond a single specialist's skill set.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific SoC's isolation architecture (e.g., secure/non-secure memory mapping), which is vendor-confidential.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access to the target chip for fault injection is only available during dedicated bench sessions, not opportunistically in the field.

equipment.rationale: Hardware-level bypass of TrustZone-style isolation typically requires advanced fault injection or SoC decapsulation equipment.

controls.name: Secure RAM
controls.description: Secure RAM is a protected memory region within an ECU or SoC that is isolated from the main system. It is used to store sensitive data such as keys or tokens during runtime to prevent memory dumping and side-channel attacks.

elapsedTime.rationale: Extracting data from protected RAM regions via cold-boot or fault-injection techniques requires sustained physical-attack effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Extracting data from protected RAM regions typically requires fault injection or cold-boot style physical attacks, requiring genuine hardware-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific SoC's secure-RAM partitioning and access-control configuration, which is not publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access to dump or glitch the RAM is generally only available during dedicated bench sessions with the device open.

equipment.rationale: Cold-boot or glitch-based RAM extraction requires bespoke physical lab equipment beyond commodity debug tools.

controls.name: Hardware Memory Protection (MPU / MMU)
controls.description: A Memory Protection Unit (MPU) or Memory Management Unit (MMU) enforces hardware-level access policies on memory regions (e.g., W^X, read-only, no-execute). Prevents shellcode injection and stack-based exploitation by ensuring code cannot be written to executable regions and data regions cannot be treated as executable. Critical W^X enforcement for RTOS and bare-metal ECUs where no OS-level ASLR exists.

elapsedTime.rationale: Bypassing hardware-enforced W^X protection via a kernel exploit or fault injection requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Bypassing MPU requires a kernel/hypervisor exploit to reconfigure protection regions, or physical fault injection to corrupt the MPU register state.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific MPU/MMU region configuration for the target RTOS/ECU, which is proprietary firmware design detail.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A kernel-level logical bypass can be attempted whenever the device is running; only physical fault injection meaningfully narrows the timing window.

equipment.rationale: Physical bypass requires voltage/clock glitch equipment; logical bypass uses only standard IT tools.

controls.name: Hypervisor and Container Isolation
controls.description: A Type-1 hypervisor or OCI-compliant container runtime enforces hardware-backed execution isolation between VMs and containers running on HPCs, preventing a compromised Infotainment VM from accessing ADAS or safety-critical partitions. This is the primary lateral-movement barrier in modern zonal E/E architectures (e.g., on NVIDIA DRIVE, Qualcomm SA8xxx).

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding and weaponizing a hypervisor escape, whether a VMM zero-day or hardware-assisted fault, requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Hypervisor escapes require a zero-day in the VMM itself or hardware-assisted fault injection - both demand elite expertise not commonly available.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires deep knowledge of the specific hypervisor/VMM's memory-management and inter-partition communication implementation, which is vendor-proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The hypervisor's attack surface (hypercalls, virtual device emulation) is reachable whenever the Infotainment VM is running, without a special timing constraint.

equipment.rationale: Software-only hypervisor escapes use standard IT equipment; hardware-assisted fault injection would require additional bespoke gear.

controls.name: Trusted Key Management
controls.description: Trusted Key Management encompasses the secure generation, distribution, storage, rotation, and destruction of cryptographic keys in automotive systems. This is a foundational control refined by specific storage implementations.

elapsedTime.rationale: Generic key-management defeat (extraction or unauthorized modification of key material) requires sustained effort in the absence of a specific stronger storage mechanism.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine applied-security expertise in key-management practices (rotation, storage, access control) to find and exploit a weakness.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the OEM's specific key lifecycle design (generation, distribution, rotation policy), which is proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: As a generic/process-level control, logical access to key-management interfaces is not meaningfully time-restricted beyond normal device operation.

equipment.rationale: Practical key extraction against a generic (non-hardware-rooted) implementation typically requires basic physical access tools (debug probes) beyond pure software.

controls.name: Encrypted Key Storage
controls.description: Ensures that cryptographic keys are encrypted or cryptographically wrapped when stored on non-volatile storage mediums. This prevents plaintext key extraction via direct logical or physical access to the storage component.

elapsedTime.rationale: Recovering a wrapped key requires either breaking the wrapping cipher or extracting the wrapping key itself, both taking sustained effort.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Recovering a wrapped key requires either breaking the wrapping cipher or extracting the wrapping key itself, both genuine cryptographic engineering tasks.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific key-wrapping scheme and where the wrapping key itself is rooted, which is implementation-proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Storage can be dumped and attacked offline once physical/logical access to the medium is obtained, with no further live-access constraint.

equipment.rationale: Extracting the raw storage image typically requires basic flash/EEPROM read-out equipment.

controls.name: Hardware Security Module (HSM)
controls.description: A Hardware Security Module (HSM) is a dedicated on-chip or discrete component designed to securely manage keys and accelerate cryptographic operations. In ECUs, HSMs provide a robust hardware root of trust.

elapsedTime.rationale: A certified automotive HSM is specifically designed to resist logical and moderate physical attack for the vehicle's operational lifetime; practical defeat exceeds a 6-month effort.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Defeating HSM tamper-resistance (fault injection, differential power analysis) requires a team with both hardware-security and cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific HSM's command interface, key-slot architecture, and firmware, which is vendor-confidential.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access for fault-injection attempts is only available during dedicated bench sessions with the ECU removed from the vehicle.

equipment.rationale: Bypassing a modern automotive HSM physically requires advanced fault injection or decapsulation gear.

controls.name: Trusted Platform Module (TPM)
controls.description: A TPM is a specialized discrete chip providing hardware-based security functions, including platform integrity measurement (PCRs) and secure key storage. Often connected via SPI/I2C in automotive gateways or HPCs.

elapsedTime.rationale: Exploiting TPM command-interface flaws or bus-level key extraction requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting TPM command interface flaws or bus-level key extraction requires genuine embedded-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific PCR measurement chain and TPM command sequence configured by the OEM.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Bus sniffing between SoC and discrete TPM requires physical access during an active boot/attestation sequence, which is not always accessible in the field.

equipment.rationale: Bus sniffing (SPI/I2C) between the SoC and discrete TPM requires basic logic analyzers and PCB access.

controls.name: Secure Element
controls.description: A secure element is a tamper-resistant hardware component dedicated to storing cryptographic keys and executing sensitive operations (e.g., V2X credentials, digital keys). Similar to TPMs but heavily hardened against physical attacks.

elapsedTime.rationale: Secure elements are specifically designed to thwart physical decapsulation and side-channel analysis for the device's operational lifetime.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Secure elements are specifically designed to thwart physical decapsulation and SCA, requiring elite expertise to crack.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Defeating a certified secure element's physical countermeasures (active shielding, sensor meshes, redundant computation) requires knowledge of that specific chip's proprietary countermeasure design - information available only to the silicon vendor and not obtainable through generic reverse engineering.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical decapsulation and probing require dedicated lab access to the extracted chip, unavailable during normal in-field opportunities.

equipment.rationale: Requires FIB/decapsulation and differential-power-analysis lab equipment to attempt physical key extraction.

controls.name: One-Time Programmable (OTP) Memory
controls.description: OTP memory is non-volatile storage that can be programmed only once. Used to securely store immutable data such as hardware root keys, device identifiers, or secure boot configuration.

elapsedTime.rationale: Altering or extracting from programmed OTP bits requires fault-injection or direct physical modification effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Altering programmed OTP bits requires fault-injection or direct physical modification expertise beyond standard embedded exploitation.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific OTP bit layout and what each fuse controls, which is proprietary to the SoC vendor/OEM.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access to the die for fault injection or direct probing is only available during dedicated bench sessions.

equipment.rationale: Physically altering OTP-programmed bits typically requires fault-injection or decapsulation-class lab equipment.

controls.name: eFuses
controls.description: eFuses are hardware-based, programmable fuses used to permanently store security-critical information or permanently disable hardware debug ports (e.g., JTAG) in production.

elapsedTime.rationale: Physically altering a blown eFuse via FIB requires sustained lab effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Physically altering a blown eFuse via FIB requires a rare combination of semiconductor failure-analysis and reverse-engineering expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific eFuse bank's physical location and bit-mapping on that SoC's die, which is proprietary vendor design data.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: FIB-based physical modification requires the chip to be decapsulated and mounted in a lab, an opportunity unavailable outside a dedicated physical-attack session.

equipment.rationale: Physically altering a blown eFuse requires focused ion beam (FIB) decapsulation equipment.

controls.name: Physical Unclonable Function (PUF)
controls.description: A PUF exploits microscopic manufacturing variations in silicon to derive a unique, unclonable device fingerprint used as a hardware root-of-trust for key derivation, without storing static key material in NVM. Eliminates the primary attack surface of key extraction from flash/EEPROM. Particularly valuable for device identity and secure provisioning.

elapsedTime.rationale: Cloning a PUF response requires chip decapsulation and advanced physical characterization - infeasible within operational attack windows.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires semiconductor-level expertise to characterize and model silicon process variation patterns.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific PUF architecture (SRAM PUF, ring-oscillator PUF, etc.) implemented on that SoC to know what to characterize and model, information not disclosed by the vendor.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical characterization requires the chip to be decapsulated and measured in a controlled lab environment, unavailable during normal field access.

equipment.rationale: Requires FIB/SEM-class laboratory equipment for silicon physical characterization; not accessible to most attackers.

controls.name: Secure Manufacturing & Key Provisioning
controls.description: Secures the factory-floor injection of initial device identity keys, certificates, and root-of-trust seed material during ECU production: HSM-mediated key generation and injection inside a controlled, access-logged provisioning cell; physical and procedural anti-tamper controls on the production line and test jigs; and cryptographic binding of each injected key set to the device's unique serial number/UID to prevent key reuse or substitution across units. Distinct from C.08.1–C.08.6, which secure keys once they are already resident and operating in a deployed vehicle; this control secures the one-time trust-establishment event that precedes deployment, as required by ISO/SAE 21434 Clause 12 (Production).

elapsedTime.rationale: Compromising a controlled, access-logged provisioning line to inject or substitute rogue key material requires sustained insider access or a supply-chain intrusion, not a single visit.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific provisioning workflow, HSM key-injection ceremony, and test-jig protocol used on that particular production line.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires insider knowledge of the factory provisioning process, which is not publicly documented and varies by Tier-1/OEM.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The provisioning event happens once per device at a single, physically controlled manufacturing site - an extremely narrow and tightly monitored window compared to attacking a device already in the field.

equipment.rationale: Requires either compromising the OEM/Tier-1's HSM-mediated provisioning tooling or gaining physical access to production-line test jigs - not commodity equipment.

controls.notes: Complements C.08.1–C.08.6 (runtime key storage/rotation) by securing the upstream trust-establishment event. Denies capabilities related to T.01.4 (Counterfeit or Rogue Hardware Integration) and T.09.8 (Supply Chain Compromise).

controls.name: HSM-Backed Code Signing (Non-Exportable Signing Keys)
controls.description: Firmware and update signing keys are generated and kept inside a backend HSM and can never be exported; every signing request is authorised by a separate release workflow (multi-person approval). Stealing the key is not possible; an attacker has to take over the signing service and its approval policy to get malicious firmware signed.

elapsedTime.rationale: Compromising a signing service with multi-person approval takes months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires expertise in backend intrusion and HSM / PKI operations.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Signing workflows are internal and restricted.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Signing requests are rare and monitored.

equipment.rationale: Standard intrusion tooling.

controls.name: Access Control
controls.description: Base mechanism restricting access to resources and operations based on policies or system attributes. Protects against unauthorized logical access and privilege escalation from within the software environment.

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding a logic flaw or misconfiguration in a generic access-control implementation typically takes a few weeks of targeted testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic privilege-escalation and access-control bypass techniques are well documented and require limited specialist skill for a generic implementation.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific access-control policy/configuration in place, which is restricted operational detail rather than deeply proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The access-control checks are enforced continuously whenever the system is running, so there is no narrow timing window to exploit.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software tools; no specialized hardware is required.

controls.name: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
controls.description: Restricts system access based on assigned roles. Commonly used for managing access to diagnostic tools, firmware updates, and cloud backend resources.

elapsedTime.rationale: Exploiting role-assignment misconfigurations or role-confusion typically takes a few weeks of targeted probing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting role-assignment misconfigurations or role-confusion is a well-documented technique requiring modest skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific role hierarchy and permission mapping deployed, which is restricted operational configuration.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: RBAC checks are enforced on every access attempt, so exploitation is not tied to a narrow timing window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software/API tooling.

controls.name: Discretionary Access Control (DAC)
controls.description: Allows resource owners to determine access (e.g., standard Linux file permissions). Prone to misconfiguration and is often bypassed by basic local privilege escalation.

elapsedTime.rationale: Local privilege-escalation exploits against standard Unix permission misconfigurations are well documented and quick to apply.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Local privilege escalation exploiting standard Unix permission misconfigurations is a widely documented, low-skill technique.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires only generic knowledge of common DAC misconfiguration patterns (world-writable files, SUID binaries), not target-specific secrets.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once local code execution is achieved, DAC bypass can be attempted at any time without further access constraints.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard shell/scripting tools already present on the target OS.

controls.name: Mandatory Access Control (MAC)
controls.description: Enforces strict, system-determined access policies (e.g., SELinux, AppArmor). Prevents compromised apps from breaking out of their containment even if running as root.

elapsedTime.rationale: Bypassing MAC usually requires discovering a zero-day kernel exploit or finding a poorly written policy.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Bypassing MAC usually requires discovering a zero-day kernel exploit or finding a poorly written policy.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific policy rules deployed (often more restrictive than public reference policies), but not deeply confidential design information.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: MAC policy is enforced continuously whenever the system runs, so exploitation is not tied to a narrow window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software exploitation tools.

controls.name: Allowlisting
controls.description: Allows only explicitly approved entities (apps, IPs, CAN IDs) to execute or transmit. Highly effective at preventing unauthorized code execution.

elapsedTime.rationale: As a default-deny mechanism, the attacker cannot simply find a gap in coverage as with RBAC/denylisting; they must smuggle a payload inside an already-approved entity, which takes sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Living-off-the-land abuse of an approved entity (rather than simple evasion) requires genuine understanding of the target's approved toolset and how to weaponize it.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of which entities are on the approved list, discoverable through observation of normal operation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The allowlist is enforced continuously during operation; no special timing is needed.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software tooling.

controls.name: Denylisting
controls.description: Blocks known malicious entities (e.g., known bad IPs, banned app hashes). Weak control easily bypassed by altering signatures or network addresses.

elapsedTime.rationale: Modifying a binary to change its hash takes seconds.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Trivially re-encoding or repacking a known-bad binary to evade a static denylist requires only modest skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Evading a signature/hash denylist by trivially modifying the binary is a generic technique requiring no knowledge of the specific denylist's contents or the target implementation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The evasion (re-hashing a malicious binary) can be prepared entirely offline before ever touching the target system.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with any standard file-editing or packing tool.

controls.name: Secure Boot
controls.description: Ensures that only firmware and software images with valid digital signatures from trusted authorities are allowed to execute during system startup, establishing a chain of trust.

elapsedTime.rationale: Requires either stealing the OEM signing key or using advanced voltage/clock glitching to skip the verification instruction - both exceed a 6-month practical effort.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires either stealing the OEM signing key or using advanced voltage/clock glitching to skip the verification instruction.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Defeating secure boot requires either the OEM's private signing key (a maximally confidential secret held in a restricted HSM ceremony) or precise knowledge of the SoC's proprietary boot-ROM verification timing to glitch - neither obtainable through public documentation or generic reverse engineering.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Voltage/clock glitching must be performed during the narrow boot-time verification window, and physical access is typically only available during dedicated bench sessions.

equipment.rationale: Fault-injection glitching to bypass boot-time signature verification requires bespoke voltage/clock-glitch rigs.

controls.name: Filesystem Integrity
controls.description: Ensures files and directories on ECUs have not been tampered with. Critical for detecting offline modifications, rootkits, and protecting static configuration data.

elapsedTime.rationale: Tampering with files while evading integrity verification requires sustained effort measured in months to find an unprotected path.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Tampering with files while evading integrity verification (e.g., via TOCTOU races or finding unprotected files) requires genuine systems-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of which files/partitions are covered by integrity verification and which are not, information specific to the OEM's build configuration.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Offline tampering (e.g., via a removed storage medium) can be attempted at leisure without a live timing constraint; detection occurs at next boot/mount.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard flashing/imaging tools once storage access is obtained.

controls.name: DM-verity (Device Mapper Verity)
controls.description: Kernel feature that provides transparent integrity checking of block devices using Merkle trees. Detects offline tampering of the read-only root filesystem and blocks the tampered image from being mounted.

elapsedTime.rationale: Bypassing the Merkle-tree verification (e.g., corrupting the root-hash trust anchor) requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Bypassing the Merkle-tree verification (e.g., corrupting the root hash trust anchor) requires genuine kernel/storage-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: dm-verity is a public Linux kernel feature; the only restricted knowledge is where the root hash is anchored (bootloader args, OTP) for this specific device.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Offline image tampering can be prepared at leisure; the verification only triggers at the next mount/boot, giving no live timing constraint.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard disk-imaging tools once storage access is obtained.

controls.name: DM-integrity (Device Mapper Integrity)
controls.description: Provides transparent integrity protection for block devices by storing and verifying checksums for each data block. Defends against offline tampering and data corruption.

elapsedTime.rationale: Corrupting a data block while producing a valid checksum requires sustained effort measured in months to understand and defeat the specific construction.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Corrupting a data block while producing a valid checksum requires understanding the specific checksum/HMAC construction used by dm-integrity.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: dm-integrity is a public Linux kernel feature; only the specific checksum algorithm/mode configured is restricted knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Offline tampering can be attempted at leisure once storage access is obtained; detection occurs on next read, not tied to a live window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard disk-imaging tools.

controls.name: Filesystem Encryption
controls.description: Protects confidentiality of files and directories by encrypting data at rest. Ensures sensitive PII, configurations, or credentials cannot be read if physical storage is dumped or stolen.

elapsedTime.rationale: Bypass requires physical extraction of RAM (cold boot) or advanced SoC decapsulation to find the encryption key, taking sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Extracting the filesystem encryption key via cold-boot RAM extraction or SoC decapsulation requires genuine hardware-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific key-derivation and storage scheme (e.g., where the master key is rooted) used by the target implementation.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once physical possession of the storage/device is obtained, key-extraction attempts can proceed without further live-access constraints.

equipment.rationale: Bypass requires physical extraction of RAM (cold boot) or advanced SoC decapsulation to find the encryption key.

controls.name: DM-crypt
controls.description: Transparent disk encryption subsystem in Linux. Often used with LUKS to manage the master key dynamically. Mitigates offline data extraction.

elapsedTime.rationale: Recovering the LUKS master key via cold-boot RAM extraction or brute-forcing a weak passphrase takes sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Recovering the LUKS master key via cold-boot RAM extraction or brute-forcing a weak passphrase requires genuine applied-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: dm-crypt/LUKS is a public Linux subsystem; only the specific key-slot configuration and passphrase/key-derivation policy are restricted knowledge.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once the device is in the attacker's possession, key-extraction attempts proceed offline without further timing constraints.

equipment.rationale: Cold-boot RAM extraction or offline brute-forcing requires basic physical memory-dumping equipment beyond pure software.

controls.name: Firmware Image Encryption
controls.description: Firmware images are encrypted at rest in flash and in update packages, and decrypted only inside the ECU with a key held in its HSM. Dumping the flash or downloading an update no longer yields readable code to reverse engineer; the attacker needs the decryption key or a fault during decryption.

elapsedTime.rationale: Extracting the image key or glitching the decryption takes weeks.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires hardware-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Key storage and boot flow of the ECU must be known.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access to the ECU for a long time.

equipment.rationale: Fault-injection or side-channel equipment.

controls.name: Authenticated Diagnostics
controls.description: Requires cryptographic authentication (e.g., UDS 0x27 SecurityAccess or 0x29 Authentication) before allowing critical diagnostic functions, preventing unauthorized reprogramming, actuator control, or data extraction.

elapsedTime.rationale: Bypassing UDS SecurityAccess (seed-key algorithm) via reverse engineering or brute-forcing the key derivation takes sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Bypassing UDS SecurityAccess (seed-key algorithm) requires genuine reverse-engineering and cryptographic expertise to derive or brute-force the key from the seed.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific seed-key algorithm implemented by the OEM/Tier-1 for that ECU, which is proprietary and not published.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The diagnostic interface is reachable whenever the vehicle is powered and a diagnostic session is requested; no special timing beyond that is needed.

equipment.rationale: A standard OBD-II/DoIP diagnostic interface and PC suffice; no specialized hardware is required for a logical seed-key attack.

controls.name: Secure Debug Interface
controls.description: Restricts, cryptographically locks, or physically disables hardware debug ports (JTAG/SWD) in production vehicles. Defends against physical firmware dumping, memory manipulation, and logic bypassing.

elapsedTime.rationale: Re-enabling disabled JTAG pins or bypassing authenticated debug modes often requires board-level micro-soldering, fault injection, or SoC decapsulation.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Re-enabling disabled JTAG pins or bypassing authenticated debug modes often requires board-level micro-soldering, fault injection, or SoC decapsulation.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific debug-authentication challenge-response scheme or fuse configuration used to lock the port, which is vendor-proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access to the board for micro-soldering or fault injection is only available during a dedicated bench session, not opportunistically in the field.

equipment.rationale: Board-level rework and fault injection require bespoke lab equipment (hot-air rework stations, glitch rigs).

controls.name: Logging and Audit
controls.description: Records security-relevant events in a tamper-evident manner. Acts as a detective control and supports non-repudiation. Forces attackers to operate stealthily or expend resources scrubbing their presence.

elapsedTime.rationale: Once privileged access is obtained, scrubbing or falsifying tamper-evident logs without detection takes a few weeks of careful operational tradecraft.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic log tampering or deletion techniques, once privileged access is obtained, require limited specialist skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific log storage location and format, discoverable through reconnaissance rather than deeply proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once privileged access is obtained, log tampering can be attempted at any time without further access restriction; the control's forensic value is what raises attacker cost, not access timing.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard shell/file-manipulation tools once access is obtained.

controls.name: Secure Software Lifecycle Management
controls.description: Ensures security is integrated into the SDLC (threat modeling, secure code reviews, CI/CD pipelines). Acts as a process control that reduces the baseline probability of software vulnerabilities existing in production.

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding zero-day logic flaws in heavily modeled and reviewed software takes exponentially more time.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Finding a residual zero-day logic flaw that survives threat modeling, secure code review, and CI/CD security gates requires genuine vulnerability-research expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires only generic vulnerability-research knowledge of common weakness classes; no confidential information about the target's internals is needed beyond what's discoverable through black-box testing/binary analysis.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: As a process control shaping what ships, it does not restrict the attacker's window to search for a residual flaw once the software is deployed; the search can proceed offline against a firmware image indefinitely.

equipment.rationale: Vulnerability research against shipped software is achievable with standard reverse-engineering and fuzzing tools.

controls.name: Software Testing
controls.description: Systematic process (fuzzing, SAST/DAST, hardware-in-the-loop pen testing) to identify memory corruption, state exhaustion, and logic defects before deployment.

elapsedTime.rationale: If a target is heavily fuzzed during testing, the remaining vulnerabilities are deeply buried and hard to trigger.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires elite exploit development to find chains the automated testing missed.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires generic vulnerability-research knowledge of the target's binary/protocol surface, obtainable through black-box analysis rather than confidential design documents.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The search for a residual, untested defect can proceed offline against an extracted firmware image at the attacker's own pace, with no live access-window constraint.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard fuzzing and reverse-engineering tooling.

controls.name: Vulnerability Management
controls.description: Ongoing process of monitoring, patching, and remediating known security vulnerabilities (CVEs) and maintaining a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM). Protects against N-day exploits.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forces the attacker to develop a novel 0-day rather than utilizing off-the-shelf exploit scripts against a known CVE.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Forces the attacker to develop a novel 0-day rather than utilizing off-the-shelf exploit scripts.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires only knowledge of the target's software/component versions (an SBOM query or version-fingerprinting), not confidential source-level detail.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Once a component is identified as unpatched, exploitation can typically be attempted whenever the target service is reachable, without further timing constraint.

equipment.rationale: Version fingerprinting and 0-day development use standard reverse-engineering tools.

controls.name: Secure Firmware Update
controls.description: Mechanisms (like cryptographically authenticated OTA client daemons) ensuring only integrity-checked firmware from the OEM is installed. Defends against malicious flashing over logical channels.

elapsedTime.rationale: Crafting or substituting a firmware image that passes the OTA client's integrity/authenticity checks requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Crafting or substituting a firmware image that passes the OTA client's integrity/authenticity checks requires genuine cryptographic and update-protocol expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific OTA update protocol, manifest format, and signature-verification chain used by the OEM, which is proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The forged/substituted image must be delivered during an active update session before the legitimate update completes, bounding the available window.

equipment.rationale: A purely logical/network-level attack against the update mechanism; no specialized hardware is required.

controls.name: Anti-Rollback Protection
controls.description: Prevents the installation of older, vulnerable firmware versions. Utilizes hardware monotonic counters (e.g., in TPMs/HSMs) or blown eFuses to enforce version minimums.

elapsedTime.rationale: Bypassing a hardware monotonic counter logically or by physical fuse manipulation requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Bypassing a hardware monotonic counter logically (e.g., counter-check race conditions) requires genuine embedded-security expertise even before resorting to physical fuse manipulation.
