knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific counter/fuse scheme (which HSM/TPM register or eFuse bank enforces the version minimum) used by the target.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physical access to decapsulate and alter fuses/NVRAM is only available during a dedicated bench session, not opportunistically.

equipment.rationale: Bypassing hardware-enforced rollback usually requires decapsulating the chip and altering the eFuses or NVRAM directly via physical means.

controls.name: Crypto-Agility / Algorithm Migration Readiness
controls.description: The architectural capability to replace a broken, deprecated, or quantum-vulnerable cryptographic algorithm - or to widen a key size - across the fleet via a software/OTA update alone, without a hardware or silicon respin. Achieved through algorithm-negotiation abstraction layers (crypto-provider interfaces that decouple protocol logic from a specific primitive), updatable/pluggable software crypto libraries, and externally configurable key-size and algorithm-selection parameters. Distinct from adopting any single algorithm such as ML-KEM (C.03.7.2) or ML-DSA (C.05.4); this control is the migration capability itself, ensuring the fleet is never permanently locked into a cryptographic primitive that a future cryptanalytic advance - classical or quantum - renders unsafe.

elapsedTime.rationale: By enabling a fleet-wide OTA rollout of a replacement algorithm once a primitive is publicly broken, this control collapses the exploitation window from the multi-year hardware lifecycle a respin would take down to a single patch cycle, forcing an attacker to weaponize and exploit the break at scale before remediation lands.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Does not raise the bar to break the underlying primitive itself - that remains whatever the cryptanalysis requires - but it does deny the attacker any durable advantage from having broken it.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: The migration abstraction layer is a build/deployment mechanism, not a security boundary the attacker interacts with or needs to study directly.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Bounds the fleet-wide exposure window after a public cryptographic break to the OEM's OTA remediation cadence rather than leaving it open for the remaining service life of the hardware.

equipment.rationale: The control is a software/build-pipeline capability; it introduces no new physical equipment requirement on either the defending or attacking side.

controls.notes: This is the migration capability itself, not an algorithm choice; compare to concrete primitive controls such as C.03.7.2 (ML-KEM) and C.05.4 (ML-DSA).

controls.name: Staged/Canary Fleet Rollout with Automatic Rollback
controls.description: Deploys OTA updates first to a small canary subset of the fleet, monitoring real-world telemetry, crash, and error-rate signals before progressively expanding to larger rollout waves, combined with dual-bank (A/B) partition updates that automatically revert to the last-known-good image if the new image fails to boot. Contains the blast radius of a bad push - whether malicious (e.g. the fleet-wide firmware propagation modeled by T.01.3) or an unintentional regression - to a small fraction of the fleet rather than the entire install base at once. Distinct from C.16.3 (Secure Firmware Update), which verifies an update's authenticity and integrity before installation, and C.16.4 (Anti-Rollback Protection), which blocks installation of an older, previously-superseded version: neither control limits how far a single authentic, non-downgraded, but nonetheless bad update is allowed to propagate before its effects are observed and stopped. This is standard practice in software-defined-vehicle update architectures.

elapsedTime.rationale: An attacker must either compromise the rollout-orchestration control plane directly or successfully evade canary-stage telemetry monitoring for long enough that a bad update advances past the canary gate - achievable with sustained effort but not a quick, single-attempt bypass.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires understanding of the specific staged-rollout orchestration logic and health-check criteria used to gate wave advancement, to either falsify telemetry or force premature advancement to the next wave.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires proprietary knowledge of the OEM's specific canary cohort selection, telemetry health thresholds, and rollout-wave cadence - none of which is publicly documented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The staged-rollout gate is a persistent architectural feature the attacker can probe and attempt to defeat at any rollout cycle, not a narrow one-time window.

equipment.rationale: A purely logical attack against the rollout-orchestration or telemetry pipeline; no specialized hardware is required.

controls.notes: The automatic-rollback half of this control mirrors Android's documented A/B seamless-update behavior: 'If an OTA update is applied but fails to boot, the device will reboot back into the old partition and remains usable.' The staged/canary-wave half is standard SDV fleet-operations practice (cf. Uptane framework deployment guidance and ISO 24089 software update engineering lifecycle management), containing exactly the fleet-wide propagation mechanism modeled by T.01.3 (Malicious Firmware Update Deployment) and the bricking/DoS mechanism modeled by T.05.5/T.05.6. Source: https://source.android.com/docs/core/ota/ab.

controls.name: Cryptographic Randomness Service
controls.description: Provides unpredictable, uniformly distributed random numbers necessary for generating cryptographic keys, nonces, initialization vectors (IVs), and salts across the platform.

elapsedTime.rationale: As a generic parent, without a committed hardware entropy source, statistical weaknesses in a generic RNG can often be identified within weeks of analysis.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Detecting and exploiting statistical bias in a random-number generator requires genuine applied-cryptography/statistics expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific RNG construction and seeding source used by the target implementation, which is not published.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Output samples can be collected and analyzed offline for bias without needing continuous live access to the generator.

equipment.rationale: Statistical analysis of collected output requires only standard computing resources.

controls.name: Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator (CSPRNG)
controls.description: A CSPRNG generates random numbers that are suitable for cryptographic use, ensuring unpredictability for keys, nonces, and other security parameters. It relies on a highly protected seed value.

elapsedTime.rationale: Distinguishing CSPRNG output from true randomness, or compromising the underlying seed, requires sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Distinguishing CSPRNG output from true randomness, or compromising the underlying seed, requires genuine applied-cryptography expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific CSPRNG algorithm and how/where its seed is protected, which is implementation-proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Output can be collected and analyzed offline; only direct seed-extraction requires live access to the device.

equipment.rationale: Statistical/cryptanalytic testing of collected output requires only standard computing resources.

controls.name: True Random Number Generator (TRNG)
controls.description: A hardware-based entropy source that leverages physical, non-deterministic phenomena (such as thermal noise, clock jitter, or quantum effects) to produce raw, high-entropy bits.

elapsedTime.rationale: Reducing entropy quality enough to make TRNG output predictable requires sustained physical manipulation of the chip environment.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires physical manipulation of the chip environment (e.g., extreme cooling) to reduce entropy generation.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: TRNG entropy-source designs (thermal noise, clock jitter) are commonly documented at a conceptual level; the restricted knowledge needed is the exact physical parameters to manipulate for that SoC.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Physically manipulating the chip's environment (extreme cooling, voltage manipulation) requires sustained physical access to the device, not available opportunistically in the field.

equipment.rationale: Environmental manipulation (cooling, voltage) to bias entropy generation requires specialized bench equipment beyond standard IT tools.

controls.name: Resource Management
controls.description: Allocates and controls system resources (CPU, Memory, Network) to ensure stability and prevent exhaustion.

elapsedTime.rationale: Crafting a resource-exhaustion condition that evades generic resource management takes a few weeks of targeted testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Basic resource-exhaustion techniques (fork bombs, memory leaks via malformed input) are well documented and require limited specialist skill.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific resource limits/quotas configured, restricted operational detail.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The resource-management logic is active whenever the system is running, so there is no narrow timing window to exploit.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software tools.

controls.name: Scheduling
controls.description: Manages task execution to support real-time performance and prevent CPU hogging by malicious or faulty processes.

elapsedTime.rationale: Crafting a task that monopolizes CPU time despite the scheduler takes a few weeks of targeted testing against the specific policy.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Crafting a task that monopolizes CPU time despite the scheduler requires only modest understanding of the specific scheduling policy.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific scheduling policy/priority scheme in use, restricted operational configuration.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The scheduler enforces its policy continuously during operation; exploitation is not tied to a narrow window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software tooling.

controls.name: Resource Limiting
controls.description: Enforces max usage quotas (e.g., Linux Cgroups) to prevent single processes from taking down an ECU's memory or compute availability.

elapsedTime.rationale: Finding a resource-exhaustion path not covered by the configured cgroup quotas takes a few weeks of targeted testing.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Finding a resource-exhaustion path not covered by the configured cgroup quotas requires only modest testing effort.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific quota configuration and which resource classes are covered, restricted operational detail.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Cgroup enforcement is continuous during operation; exploitation is not tied to a narrow window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software tooling.

controls.name: Replay Protection
controls.description: Prevents attackers from retransmitting previously captured valid messages or commands. Essential for remote vehicle access (KeyFob), diagnostics, and Secure Onboard Communication (SecOC).

elapsedTime.rationale: Defeating replay protection (freshness-value prediction, counter desynchronization, or replay-window manipulation) takes sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Defeating replay protection (freshness-value prediction, counter desynchronization, or replay-window manipulation) requires genuine protocol-security expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific freshness mechanism (timestamp tolerance, counter window size, nonce scheme) used by the target implementation, which is proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A captured legitimate message must be replayed within the implementation's freshness/counter-acceptance window, meaningfully bounding the opportunity.

equipment.rationale: Capturing and replaying bus traffic with correct timing requires a programmable CAN/network interface beyond a passive sniffer.

controls.name: Monotonic Counters
controls.description: Monotonic counters are non-decreasing numeric values used to track the order of events. Foundational for replay protection (SecOC) and anti-rollback protection for firmware updates.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forcing counter desynchronization or exploiting counter-overflow/reset edge cases takes sustained effort measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Forcing counter desynchronization or exploiting counter-overflow/reset edge cases requires genuine protocol-implementation expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific counter width, storage location, and reset/rollover behavior implemented by the target, which is proprietary.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The attack must occur before the legitimate counter advances past the replayed value, bounding the opportunity to a narrow operational window.

equipment.rationale: Manipulating or replaying counter-bearing frames with correct timing requires a programmable network interface beyond a passive sniffer.

controls.name: System Monitoring and Health Checks
controls.description: Continuously observing and evaluating the operational status of a system to detect anomalies or failures. Essential for maintaining system reliability and initiating safe-states before security issues can be fully exploited.

elapsedTime.rationale: Evading generic health-check thresholds (e.g., staying just under an anomaly trigger) takes a few weeks of targeted tuning.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Evading generic health-check thresholds (e.g., staying just under an anomaly trigger) requires only modest tuning effort.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the specific health-check thresholds/heuristics in use, restricted operational configuration.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Monitoring runs continuously during operation, so evasion is not tied to a narrow timing window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard software tooling to characterize and stay under detection thresholds.

controls.name: Watchdog Timer
controls.description: A Watchdog Timer (WDT) is a hardware or software mechanism that automatically resets the microcontroller or SoC if the system hangs or enters an unintended state. Crucial for mitigating denial-of-service states and recovering from transient fault injection attacks.

elapsedTime.rationale: A watchdog reset is easily triggered or, conversely, easily masked by periodically petting it; this is a well-understood, quickly-defeated timing mechanism.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Keeping a malicious process from being caught by the watchdog (by periodically petting it) or exploiting the reset for fault injection requires only modest embedded-systems knowledge.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Watchdog timer mechanisms are a standard, widely documented embedded design pattern; only the specific timeout interval is restricted, discoverable information.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: The watchdog is active continuously during operation; timing an attack around it does not require a narrow opportunity window.

equipment.rationale: Achievable with standard embedded debugging/scripting tools.

controls.name: Redundant Failover for Availability-Critical Functions
controls.description: Cross-component and cross-path redundancy - a hot/warm-standby backup ECU, or a redundant network path/secondary gateway route - that lets an availability-critical function (e.g., a braking-relevant CAN segment, a powertrain control loop) gracefully degrade to a safe/reduced mode rather than fail outright when its primary compute node or network path is disrupted by a denial-of-service condition or a hardware fault. Distinct from C.20.1 (a single node's own watchdog-triggered self-reset) and C.18.1/C.18.2 (single-node task scheduling and resource quotas); this control operates at the system level, providing an alternate path when the primary node or link itself becomes unavailable, rather than policing what runs on it.

elapsedTime.rationale: An attacker must sustain the disruption against both the primary and the redundant path/node simultaneously to achieve total loss of function, roughly doubling the sustained effort required.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires the attacker to identify and independently attack the specific failover path or backup-node topology, which is not always observable from the primary bus alone.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires detailed knowledge of the vehicle's specific redundancy architecture - which ECU/path is the standby, and what triggers failover to it.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A single-point disruption (one bus-off event or one flood) no longer suffices; both paths must be compromised within the failover detection interval.

equipment.rationale: Requires the ability to target two independent physical/logical paths at once, typically two injection points rather than one, though still with commodity tooling.

controls.notes: Denies the mechanism exploited by T.05.6 (CAN Bus-Off / Error-State Forced Disconnection Attack), and reinforces mitigation of the flooding-based DoS threats T.05.1 and T.20.4.

controls.name: V2X Security (IEEE 1609.2 / ETSI TS 103 097)
controls.description: Provides cryptographic authentication and pseudonymity for Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) messages using ECDSA / ECIES over pseudonym certificates managed by a PKI. Prevents spoofed V2I or V2V messages (e.g., fake hazard warnings, ghost vehicles) from being accepted by ADAS or traffic management systems. Aligned with SCMS (US) and CCMS (EU) architectures.

elapsedTime.rationale: Forging valid signed V2X messages requires sustained effort measured in months to obtain or derive usable pseudonym-certificate key material.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires knowledge of IEEE 1609.2 certificate structures and ECDSA to forge valid signed V2X messages.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: IEEE 1609.2 and ETSI TS 103 097 are public standards; the restricted knowledge needed is the specific pseudonym-certificate rotation policy and trust-list configuration of the target PKI, not the cryptographic scheme itself.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: A forged/replayed V2X message must be broadcast and accepted within the tight real-time window ADAS uses to act on it, and pseudonym certificates rotate frequently, bounding the opportunity.

equipment.rationale: Broadcasting forged V2X messages requires a DSRC/C-V2X radio and signing toolchain beyond standard IT equipment.

controls.name: V2X Misbehavior Detection
controls.description: Statistical and plausibility-based anomaly detection applied across the full V2X message stream attributable to a given sender or pseudonym-certificate identity - evaluating position/velocity/heading consistency against physical motion constraints, inter-message timing patterns, and cross-correlation against other sensor modalities (onboard radar/camera/LiDAR perception) - to detect both single-identity message forgery and multi-identity Sybil coordination. Distinct from C.21's pseudonym-certificate authentication, which verifies that a message's digital signature is cryptographically valid and traces to a legitimately-issued certificate: a validly-signed message from a legitimately-issued pseudonym certificate can still describe a physically implausible or coordinated-false vehicle state, which signature verification alone cannot detect. Directly denies the mechanism modeled by T.01.15 (V2X Sybil Attack / Multi-Identity Misbehavior) and complements C.21's coverage of T.01.11 (V2X Safety Message Injection).

elapsedTime.rationale: Crafting a synthetic multi-identity or single-message pattern that evades statistical/behavioral plausibility analysis - rather than merely a validly-signed message - requires sustained refinement measured in months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires genuine expertise in the specific detector's plausibility thresholds and multi-sensor correlation logic to craft telemetry that evades statistical/behavioral analysis, beyond the protocol-level forgery skill needed to defeat signature verification alone.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires proprietary knowledge of the target's specific misbehavior-detection thresholds and correlation logic (which physical-constraint checks it applies and how sensitively), not just the public V2X message format.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Must sustain a coordinated, physically-plausible pattern across the detector's full observation/analysis window, not just a single instantaneous message - tighter than the one-shot opportunity needed to defeat signature checking alone.

equipment.rationale: Requires multiple V2X radio front-ends or an SDR platform capable of modeling several physically-consistent fabricated trajectories simultaneously, beyond a single broadcast radio.

controls.notes: First child control of C.21; C.21 itself previously had no refinements. Denies the same Inject:Peripheral:ADAS capability node T.01.11 and T.01.15 both grant, providing detection-layer coverage that neither C.21's own cryptographic authentication nor any other existing control addresses for the Sybil-specific case. Reference: ETSI TR 103 460 V2.1.1 (2020-10), "Intelligent Transport Systems (ITS); Security; Pre-standardization study on Misbehaviour Detection", https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_tr/103400_103499/103460/02.01.01_60/tr_103460v020101p.pdf.

controls.name: Vehicle Security Operations Center (VSOC) & Incident Response
controls.description: Fleet-wide, cross-vehicle correlation of security telemetry - aggregating on-vehicle IDS alerts (C.03.10–C.03.12), audit logs (C.15), and backend access logs into a SIEM, enriched with external threat-intelligence feeds - to detect coordinated or fleet-scale attack campaigns that are invisible from any single vehicle's local logs. Provides SOAR-driven (Security Orchestration, Automation and Response) incident response: automated containment actions such as revoking a compromised certificate, quarantining an affected fleet segment from OTA distribution, or forcing targeted re-provisioning, alongside the human-in-the-loop escalation, forensics, and regulator/CSIRT notification workflows mandated by UN R155's post-production monitoring and response requirement. Distinct from C.15 (single-vehicle, on-board event logging) and C.03.10–C.03.12 (single-flow/single-vehicle intrusion detection); this control is the organizational capability that consumes those local signals at fleet scale and acts on them.

elapsedTime.rationale: Cross-fleet correlation surfaces low-and-slow or distributed campaigns (e.g., the same exploit rolled out against many vehicles one at a time) that would otherwise stay under any single vehicle's detection threshold, forcing an attacker toward a narrower, faster operational tempo to avoid fleet-level pattern detection.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Evading fleet-wide correlation requires the attacker to actively vary technique, timing, and targeting across a campaign - a materially higher bar than evading a single vehicle's local IDS.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of the OEM's specific SIEM correlation rules and SOAR playbooks, which are not externally observable.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Automated SOAR containment (certificate revocation, OTA quarantine) can react within the SOC's detection-to-response SLA, shrinking the window before a detected technique is blocked fleet-wide.

equipment.rationale: SIEM/SOAR correlation is a backend analytics capability; it requires no new physical equipment on either the defending or attacking side.

controls.notes: New top-level control category (no parent). Distinct from C.15 (on-board, single-vehicle logging) and C.03.10–C.03.12 (single-flow/single-vehicle intrusion detection); operationalizes the UN R155 post-production monitoring and incident-response mandate at fleet scale.

controls.name: Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM)
controls.description: Continuous or scheduled scanning of cloud backend infrastructure - storage bucket permissions, database access policies, IAM role bindings, serverless function permissions, and network security groups - against secure-configuration baselines to detect and remediate misconfigurations before they cause unauthorized data exposure or resource compromise. Distinct from network-layer segmentation (C.03.4), which protects traffic paths, and application-layer access control (C.09), which governs who can authenticate; this targets cloud-platform-native configuration drift itself, per NCSC and OWASP cloud security guidance.

elapsedTime.rationale: A determined attacker scanning for still-unremediated misconfigurations across a large cloud estate needs sustained but not extreme effort - weeks, not months, given scan/remediation cycles leave real windows open.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Exploiting a missed misconfiguration (an over-permissive IAM role, a public storage bucket) requires standard cloud security knowledge, not deep specialist skill - the hard part is finding the gap, not exploiting it once found.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of this specific cloud environment's scan cadence, baseline exceptions, and which resources are excluded from coverage - not public information.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Exploitation is bounded to the window between a misconfiguration being introduced and the next scan/remediation cycle catching it - meaningfully constrained but not negligible given realistic scan intervals.

equipment.rationale: No special equipment is required beyond standard cloud API/console access.

controls.name: Central Gateway Firewall and Domain Separation
controls.description: The central gateway only routes the messages and services its routing table allows between domains (allow-list per source, ID and service) and drops everything else. A compromised ECU in one domain cannot reach the network of another domain unless the gateway itself is compromised and its filter rules are changed, or the attacker is wired directly to the target segment behind the gateway.

elapsedTime.rationale: The attacker must take over the gateway and rewrite its rules, or reach the segment physically: weeks of work.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Gateway firmware and its rule format must be reverse engineered.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Routing tables are OEM-specific and confidential.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Remote once the gateway is compromised; physical otherwise.

equipment.rationale: Standard bus tools.

controls.name: Data Loss Prevention (DLP)
controls.description: Automated scanning of outbound data flows and bulk-export operations from back-end systems for sensitive data patterns (PII, cryptographic material, location history), combined with mandatory approval gates on data-sharing configuration changes and default redaction of sensitive fields in logs and exports. Prevents accidental over-exposure of vehicle or owner data caused by an already-authorized user's own configuration mistake - distinct from RBAC (C.09.1), which restricts who holds access, not what an authorized holder can inadvertently expose.

elapsedTime.rationale: Identifying an unmonitored export path or a DLP ruleset gap takes sustained reconnaissance of the backend's data flows, not a quick attempt.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Evading pattern-based DLP detection (e.g. obfuscating or fragmenting sensitive data to avoid signature matches) requires genuine understanding of how the specific DLP tooling classifies data.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Requires knowledge of this backend's specific DLP ruleset and coverage gaps, which is not public information.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: An already-authorized insider-adjacent actor has an ongoing, not narrowly time-bound, opportunity to attempt an unmonitored export.

equipment.rationale: No special equipment is required beyond the standard backend tooling the authorized user already has access to.

controls.name: Phishing-Resistant Multi-Factor Authentication
controls.description: Access to OEM backend, developer and diagnostic accounts requires a phishing-resistant second factor (FIDO2 / WebAuthn hardware key bound to the origin). A phished or leaked password alone no longer gives access; the attacker has to steal a live session from a device the user is logged in on, or relay the session through an attacker-in-the-middle proxy.

elapsedTime.rationale: Stealing a live session needs malware on the user's device or an AiTM proxy: weeks.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Session hijacking against origin-bound keys requires expertise.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Identity-provider behaviour is public.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Needs a logged-in session at the moment of attack.

equipment.rationale: Standard phishing / malware kits.

controls.name: Fault-Injection and Side-Channel Countermeasures
controls.description: Hardware glitch, voltage and clock monitors on the microcontroller plus software countermeasures (redundant checks, random delays, control-flow integrity on secure boot and key handling) make a single voltage, clock or EM fault fail safe instead of skipping a check. Software countermeasures stop protecting once the attacker can replace the firmware that implements them.

elapsedTime.rationale: Characterising a protected target for multi-glitch or laser attacks takes months.

specialistExpertise.rationale: Requires multiple hardware-security experts.

knowledgeOfTheItemOrComponent.rationale: Countermeasure placement is undocumented.

windowOfOpportunity.rationale: Long physical access to the board.

equipment.rationale: Laser or precise multi-glitch rigs.
